meta.title: The Lantau Project
meta.subtitle: 16 weeks, 3 finish lines, ~20,000 metres of climbing

milestones.label: Sea level to the summit of Everest. Twice.

meta.theDealMd:
You are not training to get faster. Your 13 August session ran at roughly **8.6 km/h flat-equivalent**. TransLantau50 requires **6.3 km/h flat-equivalent**. You are already quicker than your race pace.

The entire job is duration. Going from a one-hour ceiling to an eleven-hour day. That means: almost everything easy, almost everything about time on feet, and essentially zero speed work. If a session ever feels fast, you've misread it.

Everything in this plan serves 14 November. RCWT is the dress rehearsal. Suthep is what you get to enjoy afterwards.

**The One Thing:** you don't need to get faster, you need to get longer. Chat Pace. Every week. All the way to Mui Wo.

races.name: RCWT Explorer 30k
races.notesMd:
You have **11 hours** for 30km and 1,540m. You should finish in around **6h30–7h**. There is no cutoff pressure whatsoever, which is exactly why it's the perfect laboratory.

**This is not a race. Repeat it until you believe it.** The purpose is to rehearse TL50 under real conditions three weeks out, and to find out what breaks while it still costs you nothing.

Rehearse everything:
- The exact kit you'll wear at TL50
- Poles, from the start line to the finish line
- The full fuelling plan on the timer — this is your last big gut test
- Race-morning breakfast at the same time you'll eat it on 14 November
- Chat Pace throughout. If you can't hold a conversation, you're going too hard.

**Afterwards, write down three things:** what hurt, what your stomach did, and what you'd change. That list becomes your TL50 fix-list.

checkpoints.name: CP2 Yau Tong, O King Road

races.name: TransLantau50
races.notesMd:
44.5km, 2,508m, 09:00 start, **cutoff 20:00**.

⚠️ **Confirm the official intermediate cutoffs** in the runner's guide before race week. The table above is my pacing plan, not the organiser's limits, and the intermediate ones are what will actually stop you.

**Three things that will decide your day:**

1. **Chi Ma Wan comes early and it's the biggest climb block.** 838m in 12.4km, and you'll be fresh enough to attack it. Don't. Every minute you gain there costs you three at Lo Fu Tau.

2. **You pass through Mui Wo at 26.3km with 18km left.** You will be standing near the finish line, tired, with the two hardest climbs still ahead and 1,081m still to gain. Decide *now* what you're going to do at that checkpoint, because deciding then is how people quit.

3. **Sunset is around 17:40.** If you're on plan you'll be leaving Discovery Bay right as it goes dark. Headtorch on before you need it, not after.

**Fuelling:** 65g/hr on the timer, every 20 minutes, no negotiation. When you don't feel like eating is precisely when you must.

races.name: Suthep 20 Day
races.notesMd:
26km, 1,100m, 06:30 start, **cutoff 13:30 (7 hours)**.

- **Headtorch for the start** — sunrise in Chiang Mai is around 06:40, so you'll have 15 minutes of dark.
- **Halfway (~13km) by 09:30** puts you comfortably inside.
- **Target finish: around 12:30**, a full hour of buffer.
- December mornings in Chiang Mai are cool but midday warms up considerably. You'll be finishing in the heat of the day — carry more water than feels necessary for the second half.

Suthep is a *quicker* race than TL50 — 5.3 km/h flat-equivalent versus 6.3, but over 7 hours rather than 11.

Then stop, and go and enjoy Chiang Mai properly.

phases.name: Reboot
phases.blurb: The goal is the habit, not the fitness. You've just put together your most consistent block in six months. Protect that above all else.

phases.name: Building the Engine
phases.blurb: Volume climbs, everything stays easy. Poles come out. The gut goes to school.

phases.name: Going Long
phases.blurb: The hard yards. Two big Sundays and a recovery week between them. This is where the race gets won or abandoned, and where motivation historically goes to die — which is why the crew and the vertical tally matter now more than in August.

phases.name: Dress Rehearsal
phases.blurb: RCWT. Not a race — a laboratory with a finish line.

phases.name: Sharpen
phases.blurb: RCWT was your last long effort of consequence. Three weeks now to absorb it and arrive fresh. Resist the urge to cram — you cannot add fitness in three weeks, but you can absolutely subtract it by trying.

phases.name: Victory Lap
phases.blurb: You'll have TL50 fitness in the bank. The job is to hold it without digging a hole.

weeks.note: 🎯 **Quest of the Week: Recruit Your Crew.** You said other people are what keep you consistent — and right now you have nobody. This is the highest-leverage thing you will do all plan, and it expires. Find one running partner or one group before 6 September. Hong Kong's trail scene is dense; there is no version of this where the people don't exist. Post in a group, ask a colleague, turn up to a club run. Do it this week while motivation is still cheap.

protocols.title: Your Week
protocols.bodyMd:
Four running days, two strength evenings, two genuinely free days. **Saturday is free by design** — family chaos costs you nothing, and Friday plus Saturday leave you fresh for Sunday. Roughly 4–6 hours, touching 7 in Week 9.

### The default template

| Day | Lunchtime | Evening |
|---|---|---|
| **Sun** | 🥾 **The Long One** — early, before the house wakes | — |
| **Mon** | — *(no running)* | 🦶 Ankle Church + 💪 Strength, ~30 min |
| **Tue** | 🐌 The Shuffle | — |
| **Wed** | 🪜 The Grind | — |
| **Thu** | ⛰️ The Drop | 🦶 Ankle Church + 💪 Strength, ~30 min |
| **Fri** | — | Optional 🚣 easy row *(light weeks only)* |
| **Sat** | Free. 🧘 Yoga if the day allows, otherwise nothing | — |

**Monday is a deliberate rest day from running.** It sits directly after the long run, when soreness peaks and connective tissue is most vulnerable — and after three years detrained your tendons lag well behind your engine. It's also your hardest day for time, and a plan with no protected day is one you resent by October.

Days are movable within the week. What must not move: the Sunday long run, and both strength blocks.

### The sessions

**🪜 The Grind** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Stairs and hill repeats. Your weekday time slot is too short to build volume but perfect for building vertical, which is exactly what these races need. Climb hard, descend controlled, repeat. Pace is meaningless; effort is everything.

**🐌 The Shuffle** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Easy aerobic running. Flat or rolling. This is the boring one, and it is the one that builds the engine. It should feel almost embarrassingly easy. Capped at conversational effort, no exceptions.

**⛰️ The Drop** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Descent work. Find a hill, jog up easy, come down with control and quick feet. This trains the quads to absorb 2,500m of downhill without falling apart at 30km. It is the single most neglected session in trail training and the one that decides your race.

**🥾 The Long One** *(Sunday morning, early)* — The centrepiece. Start at 06:30 or 07:00 to rehearse race-morning logistics, get the fuelling timed, and beat the heat. Trails, poles, full kit, real food. Every one of them is spelled out in the Long Session Playbook.

**🦶 Ankle Church + 💪 Strength** *(Monday and Thursday evenings, ~30 min, on top)* — Paired into one block so it's two things to remember rather than four. If time is short, do the ankle work and drop the rest — never the other way round.

### Effort, not pace

Hong Kong in September makes pace numbers lie to you. Use the talk test:

- **Chat Pace** — full sentences. This is TL50 race effort. Most of your training lives here.
- **Steady** — short sentences only.
- **Hard** — single words. You'll barely use this.

Your progress metric isn't pace. It's your heart rate coming down for the same effort. Right now you're averaging 147–156bpm for modest work. Watch that drift downward over eight weeks — that's the engine being built.

protocols.title: The Long Session Playbook
protocols.bodyMd:
The Long One is the session that decides your races. Each one has a job — the app carries it on the session itself, and this is the system behind them.

### The metric that matters

**flat-equivalent km = distance (km) + climb (m) ÷ 100**
**fe speed = fe km ÷ hours**

| Race | Requires |
|---|---|
| RCWT | 4.1 km/h fe |
| **TransLantau50** | **6.3 km/h fe** |
| Suthep 20 | 5.3 km/h fe |

It's the only number directly comparable to a cutoff, and it works across any terrain. **The app calculates it for you** — log duration, distance and climb on a long run and the fe speed appears on the row.

**Targets are duration and vertical. Distance is whatever it turns out to be.** Chasing distance on Hong Kong trails leads you to flat ground, which is not what you're training for.

⚠️ **Two of your three races are on Saturdays** — RCWT on 24 October and TL50 on 14 November. Training on Sundays doesn't change the physiology, but it does mean those two Saturdays need clearing with the family now, not in October.

### Rules for every long session

1. **Start at 06:30–07:00.** All three races start in the morning. Rehearse the alarm, the breakfast, the pre-dawn stomach.
2. **Race breakfast, 2–2.5 hours before.** Same food every week. By November your gut should recognise it.
3. **Poles from Week 3.** Every long session, no exceptions, until the decision is locked after RCWT.
4. **Fuelling on a 20-minute timer from Week 3.** Eat on the beep, not by feel.
5. **Hike everything above roughly 12% gradient — deliberately, even when you could run it.**
6. **No stop longer than three minutes.** From Week 6, practise a timed "aid station" drill: stop, refill, eat, move.
7. **Last 10 minutes on technical ground from Week 9.** Rolling an ankle when tired is a trainable skill.
8. **Four lines in the log afterwards:** fe speed, what you ate and when, what your stomach did, any niggle.

### The run/hike discipline

This is the skill that wins cutoff races, and it's counterintuitive enough that most people never practise it.

You are not trying to run TL50. You're trying to **hike the climbs efficiently and run everything runnable**, for eleven hours. Someone who runs the early climbs and walks the late flats finishes slower than someone who hikes every climb and runs every descent — and is far more likely to be sick at halfway, because high intensity shuts down gastric emptying.

**Practise hiking when you feel strong enough to run.** That's the whole drill. It will feel wrong in September and it will save your race in November.

**Power-hike technique:** short steps, high cadence, torso upright rather than bent, hands driving on your quads or your poles, breathing on a rhythm. It should feel like a distinct gear, not like giving up.

**Descending technique** — you descend well, but detrained quads and a sprain history change the calculus. Shorten your stride, raise your cadence (your 133spm is low; aim to feel quicker rather than longer), land under your centre of mass rather than reaching ahead, and look three to four steps down the trail instead of at your feet. On technical ground, control speed with foot placement rather than by braking with your quads — braking is what destroys them by 30km.

### The kit ladder

**Level 1 — Weeks 1–5.** Small vest or handheld, 500ml–1L, phone, one food item. Poles from Week 3.

**Level 2 — Weeks 6–8.** Vest with 1.5L capacity, two or three food types, salt, headtorch from Week 6, poles.

**Level 3 — Week 9 onward.** **Full TL50 mandatory kit, at race weight, every single time.**

☐ Pull the mandatory gear list from the TL50 race page and buy anything missing by the end of September. A loaded pack changes your climbing rate, your shoulders, your sweat rate and your centre of gravity on descents. Discovering that on 14 November is not a plan.

### Vertical from long sessions

| Weeks | From long sessions |
|---|---|
| 1–5 | ~2,350m |
| 6–9 | ~4,130m |
| 10–13 | ~5,350m |
| 14–16 | ~2,200m |
| **Total** | **~14,000m** |

The remaining ~6,000m of your 20,000m bank comes from weekday Grind sessions.

### If a long session goes wrong

**Ran out of time.** Cut the back end, keep the climbing. 2h with 800m beats 3h with 300m for these races.

**Felt terrible from the start.** Convert it to a hike of the same duration. Time on feet is the point; running is just one way to accumulate it.

**Stomach trouble.** Don't abandon the session — run the rescue protocol (drop effort, sip dilute liquid, salty food, resume at 30–40g/hr). Practising the recovery is worth more than a clean session.

**Missed it entirely.** Try Saturday, or Monday morning if you can. If that's gone too, do not try to make it up midweek — take the shorter session and carry on. One missed long run costs you very little. Three consecutive ones cost you the race.

protocols.title: Fuelling — The Primary Objective
protocols.bodyMd:
**Two previous TL50 attempts have failed here. This is not a supporting protocol; it is the main thing this training block has to fix.**

### The three numbers

1. **You store ~1,800 kcal of glycogen.** That's the only fuel you can burn fast.
2. **You'll oxidise carbohydrate at ~250–300 kcal/hour** at race effort. Fat covers the rest and is effectively unlimited.
3. **Your gut absorbs a maximum of 60–90g carbs/hour** (~240–360 kcal), regardless of how much you swallow.

Six hours of stored fuel, an eleven-hour race, and an absorption ceiling that only just covers the burn rate *if you eat continuously from the start*. There is no spare capacity and no way to catch up.

### Why checkpoint-only fuelling fails — the mechanism

The stomach empties carbohydrate at **1–1.5g per minute**. That's a plumbing limit. 20–25g every 20 minutes sits exactly at that rate — which is where the 20-minute rule comes from.

TL50's aid stations are at 7, 19.5, 26.3 and 36km — gaps of 1h20, **2h45**, 1h25, **2h35** and 2h40. Four feeding opportunities in eleven hours means ~175g per stop, which takes over two hours to leave the stomach.

What follows is predictable: a concentrated bolus is hypertonic, so it draws water *into* the gut instead of absorbing. Sloshing, then nausea, then you stop eating. Now you're in deficit and cannot recover, because absorption is capped no matter how motivated you are. This is a strategy that fails arithmetically, not a weak stomach.

### Why training the gut actually works

The SGLT1 transporter that carries glucose across the intestinal wall is **upregulated by repeated exposure**. Two to four weeks of consistent carbohydrate intake during exercise measurably raises tolerance. The gut adapts like tissue, not like a habit. Someone who has practised for twelve weeks handles 80g/hr; the same person untrained vomits at 50g/hr.

**You have never trained the organ that failed.** That's the change this time.

### Real food vs gels

The useful variables are **osmolality** and the **glucose-to-fructose ratio**, not whether something is natural. Glucose crosses via SGLT1, saturating near 60g/hr; fructose uses GLUT5, worth another 30g/hr. Mixing roughly 2:1 gives you two pipes rather than one — which is why starch plus fruit or honey beats either alone.

**Strategy: real food for the first two-thirds, liquid and gels for the last third.** Late in a race, saliva drops, chewing becomes unpleasant, and solid food gets rejected in a way liquid doesn't. Carry 3–4 gels as insurance even if you intend never to use them.

**Avoid mid-race: fat and fibre.** Both slow gastric emptying badly. No nuts, peanut butter, chocolate, oily pastries or wholemeal anything — precisely the "healthy" foods people reach for.

**Palate fatigue is real.** Eleven hours of sweet produces genuine aversion by hour six. **Half your carbohydrate should be savoury.** This is the main advantage real food holds over gels.

| Food | Carbs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Onigiri / salted rice ball | ~40g | Savoury, salted, easy to chew. The best single option |
| Boiled baby potatoes, salted | ~7g each | Excellent savoury fuel. Carry in a zip bag |
| White bread, honey or jam | ~25g per half | Cheap, glucose + fructose |
| Medjool dates | ~18g each | Dense. Needs water alongside |
| Banana | ~25g | Slightly ripe, never green |
| Fig rolls | ~11g each | Tolerable late in a race |
| Coca-Cola | ~35g / 330ml | Genuinely useful in the final third |
| Maltodextrin drink in a soft flask | ~50g / 500ml | Carries carbs without chewing |
| Salted plums (話梅) | — | Not fuel. Palate reset and sodium |

### Sodium and fluid

**500–800mg sodium and 400–600ml fluid per hour.** Sweat losses in Hong Kong run 0.8–1.5 L/hr at 300–1,500mg sodium per litre.

The mechanism usually left out: SGLT1 is the *sodium*-glucose linked transporter — it co-transports both. Sodium isn't only about cramps; it is directly required to absorb your carbohydrate. Under-salting throttles your fuelling.

### The race plan — TL50

**Target 65g carbs/hour ≈ 700g total, plus 20% reserve.**

| Segment | Time | Carbs to carry |
|---|---|---|
| Start → Ham Tin | 1h20 | ~85g |
| Ham Tin → Chi Ma Wan | 2h45 | **~180g** |
| Chi Ma Wan → Mui Wo CP | 1h25 | ~90g |
| Mui Wo CP → Discovery Bay | 2h35 | ~170g |
| Discovery Bay → Finish | 2h40 | ~175g |

**Rules on the day:**

- **First feed at 30 minutes.** Not when hungry — hunger is a lagging indicator and by the time you feel it you're already behind.
- **Timer every 20 minutes.** Three feeds an hour, 20–25g each. Eat on the beep. This is the single change that fixes your previous two attempts.
- **Aid stations top up your supplies. They do not replace carrying your own.**
- Drink alongside every solid feed.
- ☐ **Check whether a drop bag is allowed at the Mui Wo checkpoint (26.3km)** — it's the start/finish area, and if so it halves what you carry early.

### Your specific failure mode: delayed gastric emptying

Both attempts ended with nausea and vomiting at around halfway. That timing points at the Chi Ma Wan aid station — arriving at ~4 hours, behind and hungry, eating a large amount, and bringing it back up 30–60 minutes later.

This is **not** a food intolerance. Intolerances present in the first hour or two. This is the stomach failing to empty: blood is diverted from the gut to muscle and skin during exercise, splanchnic flow drops by 20–80%, contents accumulate, and eventually the accumulated volume comes back up. The food didn't disagree with you. It never left your stomach.

**Four levers, in order of importance for your case:**

**1. Effort.** Gastric emptying works reasonably below ~70% of max HR and collapses above ~80%. The hour before your nausea began was the Chi Ma Wan peninsula — 838m in 12.4km, the biggest climbing block of the race, early enough that you'd still feel strong. **Going too hard on Chi Ma Wan is what makes you vomit at Mui Wo.** Hike the climbs. Hold Chat Pace. Arrive at 19.5km feeling like you're going too slowly. Pacing is a fuelling intervention.

**2. Delivery rate.** Never a bolus. 20–25g every 20 minutes, matched to the 1–1.5g/min emptying rate. Arrive at aid stations already fuelled and only top up — never arrive starving and stuff yourself.

**3. Hydration.** Low plasma volume makes the body divert even more blood away from the gut. Under-drinking in the first three hours compounds the problem before you feel anything. 400–600ml/hr from the first 20 minutes, not from when you feel thirsty.

**4. Concentration.** Keep drink mixes at 6–8% carbohydrate (60–80g/litre). Above ~10% emptying slows sharply. Dilute further than the packet says. Cold fluids empty marginally faster, which also helps thermally.

**No NSAIDs.** Ibuprofen and similar reduce gut blood flow and increase intestinal permeability — they make this exact failure more likely. If they're part of your race routine, remove them.

### 🚨 The rescue protocol — when nausea starts

**Do not stop eating.** Stopping is what converts nausea into a DNF. The correct response reduces load on the gut while keeping fuel going in:

1. **Drop your effort right down for 15–20 minutes.** Walk. This restores gut blood flow and is the fastest-acting intervention available to you.
2. **Switch from solids to sipping.** Dilute drink or flat cola, small sips, continuously.
3. **Take something salty** — salted plums, crisps, broth at an aid station.
4. **Resume at reduced intake** — 30–40g/hr — rather than resuming at zero.
5. **Ginger** in any form is worth carrying. Modest evidence, no downside.

You have 11 hours. Losing 30 minutes to a walking recovery costs you far less than the deficit you cannot repay. Nausea is recoverable; an empty stomach at hour eight is not.

### Testing schedule

| When | Target | What to test |
|---|---|---|
| Weeks 3–4 | 30g/hr | Two foods only. Establish a baseline that doesn't upset you |
| Weeks 5–6 | 40–50g/hr | Introduce a savoury option. Start the 20-min timer habit |
| Week 7 (3h45) | 50–60g/hr | Full race kit. Test carrying it, not just eating it |
| Week 9 (5h30) | 65–75g/hr | The exact race plan, on the actual course |
| Week 10 (RCWT) | 65g/hr | Full dress rehearsal. **Last day anything new is allowed** |
| Week 12 | 65g/hr | Confirm, change nothing |

**Two tests requiring no running:**

**Sweat rate.** Weigh naked, run one hour, towel off, weigh again, add back any fluid drunk. 1kg lost = 1 litre sweat. Do it once in September heat and once in November. This gives you your real hourly fluid need rather than a guess.

**Palatability at rest.** Eat the foods on the sofa first. If you can't face a rice ball there, you certainly won't at hour seven.

**Keep a one-line log after every long run:** what you took, when, and what your stomach did. By Week 9 you'll know your own answer better than any general guidance. That log is worth more than this entire section.

protocols.title: The Ankle Protocol
protocols.bodyMd:
Your sprain history is the biggest injury risk in this plan. Proprioception degrades with fatigue faster than strength does, which is why rolls happen at hour seven, not hour one — and why a confident descender with weak ankles is more at risk, not less.

Ten minutes, twice a week, paired with the strength block on Monday and Thursday evenings. Barefoot, next to a wall.

1. **Single-leg balance** — 3 × 30s each leg. Progress: eyes open → eyes closed → on a cushion, eyes closed. *Substitute freely with yoga balance postures — tree, warrior III, half moon, eagle. Identical proprioceptive stimulus, and you'll do them better and more willingly.*
2. **Eccentric heel drops** — 3 × 15 each leg, off a step, lowering slowly.
3. **Banded ankle eversion** — 3 × 15 each side. Targets the peroneals, which are what actually stop a roll.
4. **From Week 6, add: single-leg hop and stick** — 3 × 8 each leg. Land, absorb, freeze for two seconds.

Also: from Week 9, do the last ten minutes of every long run deliberately on technical ground. Rolling an ankle when tired is a trainable skill.

protocols.title: The Pole Decision
protocols.bodyMd:
You own poles and rarely use them. That's the worst position, because TL50's rules force the choice at the start line — you either carry them the whole way or you don't have them at all.

Poling is a trained skill and a trained set of muscles. Someone who picks up poles cold for an 11-hour day gets shredded lats, a slower climb rate, and hands too tired to open a gel.

- **Weeks 3 onward** — poles on every single Long One
- **Week 6** — poles on one weekday Grind
- **Week 9** — poles for the full 5h30 recce
- **Week 10** — poles at RCWT, start to finish
- **After RCWT** — decision locked, either way

Given your ankle history and 2,508m of descending, I expect the answer is yes. But test it rather than assume it.

protocols.title: Yoga
protocols.bodyMd:
**Sunday, 20–30 minutes, gentle.** Not a substitute for the strength block.

**What it won't do:** prevent injuries, or lengthen "tight" muscles. Post-climb tightness is protective neural tone and soreness, not shortened tissue — stretching relieves it by raising stretch tolerance, which is why the relief is real but temporary.

**What it will do:**

- **Balance postures are proprioception training.** Tree, warrior III, half moon, eagle — the same stimulus as the ankle protocol's balance work, done better because you have years of practice. Substitute them in.
- **Thoracic mobility** for poling. Eleven hours of pole work asks for rotation and extension through the upper back.
- **Adherence.** You enjoy it and you're good at it. Given motivation is the main risk in this plan, that counts for more than marginal exercise optimisation.

**Three cautions:**

- **Don't chase deeper ankle range.** Your history is sprains — you need stability, not flexibility. Extra passive range at a repeatedly injured joint works against you.
- **No deep static stretching straight after the long run.** The tissue has micro-damage; end-range loading isn't what it needs. Ten gentle minutes, not a deep hamstring session.
- **Skip hot yoga in heavy weeks.** Additional heat stress and fluid loss you don't need.

protocols.title: Core & Upper Body — The Poling Engine
protocols.bodyMd:
Twice weekly, ~20 minutes, at home, **paired with Ankle Church on Monday and Thursday evenings** — one 30-minute block rather than four things to remember. They're office days, so you've no trail access at lunch anyway.

Your upper-body goal and your race goal happen to align. Eleven hours on poles loads lats, triceps, shoulders and grip far harder than most people expect, and hands too tired to open a gel at 35km is a real and common failure. So this is training, not just toning.

The relevant core for trail running is **anti-rotation and lateral stability**, not crunches. Nothing in trail running looks like a sit-up; a great deal of it looks like resisting sideways collapse on one leg.

| Exercise | Sets | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Side plank** | 3 × 30–45s each side | The most trail-relevant core exercise there is — resisting lateral collapse is what your trunk does in every single-leg stance |
| **Dead bug** | 3 × 10 each side | Trunk stability with limbs moving independently |
| **Bird dog** | 3 × 10 each side | Adds the posterior chain and hip control |
| **Push-ups** | 3 × (max − 2) | Triceps and shoulders — the pole push-off |
| **Rows** (band or rowing machine) | 3 × 12 | Lats and rear delts — the pole pull. The primary poling muscles |
| **Farmer's carry** | 2 × 40m heavy | Grip and trunk under load. Transfers directly to poles |

Never skip Ankle Church for this. If time is short, do the ankles and three of the six.

protocols.title: Daily Nutrition
protocols.bodyMd:
Distinct from race fuelling. This is about maximising what you get back from the training.

**The mindset:** you are building from detrained on limited hours. Every session has to produce adaptation, and adaptation is bought with food and sleep. The risk here is under-fuelling, not over-eating — an under-fuelled build is the fastest route to both injury and the motivation crash.

**Protein — 1.6–2.0g per kg of bodyweight, daily.** Spread across four meals at 25–40g each rather than loaded at dinner. This matters more for you than for the average runner: connective tissue adaptation is what protects your ankles, and it's protein-dependent.

**Collagen + vitamin C before ankle work.** 15g of collagen or plain gelatin with 50mg vitamin C, 30–60 minutes before Ankle Church. Evidence is moderate rather than conclusive, but it's cheap, safe, and aimed squarely at your weakest link.

**Carbohydrate around the Long One.** Eat well the day before, and don't run the long one fasted while you're building. Fasted long runs are a tool for a different goal than yours.

**Low fibre for 24 hours before every Long One and every race.** This is the single highest-value item in this section given your GI history. High fibre is excellent daily nutrition and a genuine liability at hour six. Most people never connect the two.

**Recovery window.** Carbs plus protein within an hour of finishing the Long One. On the other days it matters much less than the internet suggests.

**Sodium daily, not just on race day.** Hong Kong summer sweat rates are high enough that chronic sodium depletion is a real thing. Salt your food generously through September.

**Rehearse the race breakfast every long run.** Two to two-and-a-half hours before the start, 1–2g carbs per kg, low fibre, low fat. By 14 November your stomach should recognise it.

**Caffeine.** Useful, and worth standardising rather than improvising — don't race on a dose you haven't trained with.

**Alcohol.** The night before a Long One is the one to protect. Sleep quality is where the damage is done, not the calories.

**Worth checking:** if fatigue persists disproportionately in September, ask your GP for a ferritin test. Endurance athletes lose iron, and low ferritin feels exactly like being unfit.

**And the biggest lever of all is sleep.** No supplement in this section comes close.

protocols.title: The Rowing Machine
protocols.bodyMd:
Dust it off. It's more useful than you'd think — with one hard condition: **it substitutes, it never adds.**

**What it gives you:**

- **Non-impact aerobic volume.** You can add engine without adding impact load while your tissues catch up to your ambitions. That's valuable in exactly your situation.
- **The poling muscles.** Lats, rear delts, triceps, grip — rowing trains the precise musculature you'll need on 2,500m of climbing.
- **Zero friction.** It's in your house. On the days when motivation is the binding constraint, the session you can start in thirty seconds is the only one that happens.
- **It's indoors.** Beats a September lunchtime in Hong Kong.

**What it cannot do:** eccentric quad loading, ankle proprioception, or course specificity. It will not prepare your legs for descending, which is the thing most likely to end your TL50. Treat it as a complement, never a replacement.

**How to use it:**

- **Primary role — the backup Shuffle.** Missed a lunchtime run? 25–30 minutes steady on the rower. Session saved.
- **Optional extra:** one 20-minute easy row on a non-running day, but only in weeks totalling under 5 hours.
- **Never** in Weeks 9, 13 or 16. Those are peak and taper weeks where extra load costs you more than it buys.
- **Technique:** legs → core → arms on the drive, arms → core → legs on the recovery. Keep the stroke rate low (20–24 spm) and the pressure high. High-rate flailing trains nothing.

protocols.title: The Commute Protocol
protocols.bodyMd:
Three office days, two hours of bus each — six hours a week of dead time.

Being straight with you: this is **aerobically worthless**. You cannot build endurance sitting down and I'd be making things up if I claimed otherwise. But two of these genuinely target your weak points, and they cost you nothing.

**🪑 Seated tibialis anterior raises — 3 × 25.** Heels planted, lift the toes as high as they'll go, lower slowly. The tib ant controls foot placement on descents and produces that burning shin sensation late in a long downhill. Almost nobody trains it. You have six hours a week.

**🪑 Seated soleus raises — 3 × 25.** Knees bent at 90°, press through the forefoot, heels up. Bent-knee calf raises target the soleus specifically — a major ankle stabiliser and a muscle that takes enormous load in trail running.

**🪑 Banded eversion.** Keep a mini-band in your bag. Same movement as in the ankle protocol, entirely discreet.

**🧍 Standing, if you can get a spot.** A moving bus is legitimately excellent proprioception training — unpredictable multi-directional perturbation, which is exactly what a trail delivers. Loose knees, hand near the rail but not gripping it. This is the best ankle training available on a commute, and it's free.

**🪑 Isometric bracing — 10 × 10s.** Brace the trunk as though about to be poked in the stomach, breathe normally throughout. Modest benefit, but it's genuinely dead time.

Supplementary, not foundational. Don't let it become a reason to skip anything else.

protocols.title: When It Goes Wrong
protocols.bodyMd:
It will. Here's the triage, decided in advance so you're not deciding it while demotivated:

**Missed a week.** Repeat the week you missed, don't skip ahead. One repeated week costs you almost nothing; one week of trying to catch up costs you three.

**Missed two or more weeks.** Drop back one full week in the plan and rebuild. The long run ladder is the thing to protect; weekday sessions are expendable.

**Something hurts.** Ankle, knee, or Achilles pain that changes how you move is a stop signal, not a push-through signal. Two days off early beats three weeks off later.

**Motivation gone.** This is the failure mode your history actually points to, so treat it as a foreseeable event rather than a personal failing. The response is not willpower — it's lowering the bar until something happens. Do fifteen minutes. Do the Ankle Church and nothing else. Text whoever you recruited in Week 1 and make it their problem. The plan survives bad weeks; it doesn't survive silent ones.

**Behind schedule in October.** If Week 9's 5h30 feels out of reach, TL50 is still on — but run RCWT as a genuine long day rather than a rehearsal, and revise the TL50 target from 10h45 to "make every cutoff and finish."
